Problem Statement¶

Business Context¶

Renewable energy sources play an increasingly important role in the global energy mix, as the effort to reduce the environmental impact of energy production increases.

Out of all the renewable energy alternatives, wind energy is one of the most developed technologies worldwide. The U.S Department of Energy has put together a guide to achieving operational efficiency using predictive maintenance practices.

Predictive maintenance uses sensor information and analysis methods to measure and predict degradation and future component capability. The idea behind predictive maintenance is that failure patterns are predictable and if component failure can be predicted accurately and the component is replaced before it fails, the costs of operation and maintenance will be much lower.

The sensors fitted across different machines involved in the process of energy generation collect data related to various environmental factors (temperature, humidity, wind speed, etc.) and additional features related to various parts of the wind turbine (gearbox, tower, blades, break, etc.).

Objective¶

“ReneWind” is a company working on improving the machinery/processes involved in the production of wind energy using machine learning and has collected data of generator failure of wind turbines using sensors. They have shared a ciphered version of the data, as the data collected through sensors is confidential (the type of data collected varies with companies). Data has 40 predictors, 20000 observations in the training set and 5000 in the test set.

The objective is to build various classification models, tune them, and find the best one that will help identify failures so that the generators could be repaired before failing/breaking to reduce the overall maintenance cost. The nature of predictions made by the classification model will translate as follows:

  • True positives (TP) are failures correctly predicted by the model. These will result in repairing costs.
  • False negatives (FN) are real failures where there is no detection by the model. These will result in replacement costs.
  • False positives (FP) are detections where there is no failure. These will result in inspection costs.

It is given that the cost of repairing a generator is much less than the cost of replacing it, and the cost of inspection is less than the cost of repair.

“1” in the target variables should be considered as “failure” and “0” represents “No failure”.

Data Description¶

The data provided is a transformed version of the original data which was collected using sensors.

  • Train.csv - To be used for training and tuning of models.
  • Test.csv - To be used only for testing the performance of the final best model.

Both the datasets consist of 40 predictor variables and 1 target variable.

Exploratory Data Analysis¶

Univariate analysis¶

In [20]:
# function to plot a boxplot and a histogram along the same scale.

def histogram_boxplot(data, feature, figsize=(12, 7), kde=False, bins=None):
    """
    Boxplot and histogram combined

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    figsize: size of figure (default (12,7))
    kde: whether to the show density curve (default False)
    bins: number of bins for histogram (default None)
    """
    f2, (ax_box2, ax_hist2) = plt.subplots(
        nrows=2,  # Number of rows of the subplot grid= 2
        sharex=True,  # x-axis will be shared among all subplots
        gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": (0.25, 0.75)},
        figsize=figsize,
    )  # creating the 2 subplots
    ax_box2.set_title(feature)
    sns.boxplot(
        data=data, x=feature, ax=ax_box2, showmeans=True, color="violet"
    )  # boxplot will be created and a star will indicate the mean value of the column
    sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2, bins=bins, palette="winter"
    ) if bins else sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2
    )  # For histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        data[feature].mean(), color="green", linestyle="--"
    )  # Add mean to the histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        data[feature].median(), color="black", linestyle="-"
    )  # Add median to the histogram

Variables V1 to V29¶

In [21]:
for feature in data_train.columns:
    histogram_boxplot(data_train, feature, figsize=(12, 7), kde=False, bins=None)

Univariate Observations:¶

Distributions

  • Most features (V1–V40) show approximately symmetric, bell-shaped distributions — means and medians are close across the majority of variables.
  • V3 and V35 are shifted noticeably above zero (means of 2.48 and 2.23), unlike most other features which are centered near 0.
  • V6 and V7 are consistently negative-shifted (means of -1.00 and -0.88).

Outliers

  • Nearly all features show outliers on both tails in the boxplots — extreme values extend well beyond the whiskers.
  • V32 has the widest spread (std = 5.50, range ≈ -19.9 to +23.6) and the most pronounced outliers.
  • V38 and V36 also show notably wide ranges with outlier-heavy tails.
  • These outliers likely represent abnormal sensor readings and should not be removed, as they may correspond to actual failure conditions.

Bivariate Analysis¶

Correlation Check¶

In [24]:
cols_list = data_train.select_dtypes(include=np.number).columns.tolist()
cols_list.remove("Target")

plt.figure(figsize=(20, 20))
sns.heatmap(
    data_train[cols_list].corr(), annot=True, vmin=-1, vmax=1, fmt=".2f", cmap="Spectral"
)
plt.show()

Bivariate Observations:¶

Feature-to-Feature Correlations (Heatmap)

  • There are 119 feature pairs with |r| > 0.5, indicating widespread multicollinearity across the 40 predictors.
  • The strongest correlations are:
    • V7 & V15: +0.868 (strong positive)
    • V2 & V14: -0.854 (strong negative)
    • V16 & V21: +0.837 (strong positive)
    • V24 & V32: +0.825 (strong positive)
    • V11 & V29: +0.811 (strong positive)
  • Both positive and negative high correlations exist, suggesting some sensor readings move together while others are inversely related.
  • The high degree of inter-feature correlation suggests redundancy in the feature set — several variables likely capture overlapping information from related components or sensors.

Feature-to-Target Correlations

  • No single feature has a strong individual correlation with the target. The highest is V18 at -0.293, followed by V21 (0.256), V15 (0.249), V7 (0.237), and V16 (0.231).
  • All correlations with Target are weak (< 0.30), meaning failure cannot be predicted from any one variable alone — the model will need to learn complex combinations of features.

Conclusions

  • The widespread multicollinearity may cause issues for linear models but is handled well by neural networks, which learn non-linear feature interactions automatically.
  • Since no single predictor strongly separates failure from non-failure, the classification task is genuinely complex and benefits from a deep learning approach.
  • Highly correlated feature pairs (e.g., V7 & V15, V2 & V14) could be candidates for dimensionality reduction, though for neural networks this is generally less critical than for tree-based or linear models.

Missing Value Imputation¶

  • There were few missing values in V1 and V2, we will impute them using the median.
  • And to avoid data leakage we will impute missing values after splitting train data into train and validation sets.
In [31]:
imputer = SimpleImputer(strategy="median")
In [32]:
scaler = StandardScaler()
# Fit and scale the train data
X_train = pd.DataFrame(scaler.fit_transform(X_train), columns=X_train.columns)
# Fit and scale the validation and test data
X_val   = pd.DataFrame(scaler.transform(X_val),       columns=X_train.columns)
X_test  = pd.DataFrame(scaler.transform(X_test),      columns=X_train.columns)

# Fit and transform the train data
X_train = pd.DataFrame(imputer.fit_transform(X_train), columns=X_train.columns)

# Transform the validation data
X_val = pd.DataFrame(imputer.transform(X_val), columns=X_train.columns)    # impute missing values in the validation set while accounting for data leakage

# Transform the test data
X_test = pd.DataFrame(imputer.transform(X_test), columns=X_train.columns)    # impute missing values in the test set while accounting for data leakage

Model Building¶

Model Evaluation Criterion¶

Primary metric: Recall

The costliest outcome is a False Negative — a real failure that goes undetected, resulting in full generator replacement. Since replacement costs far exceed repair costs, we want to minimize missed failures above all else. Recall (= TP / TP + FN) directly measures this.

Secondary metric: F1 Score

Recall alone could be gamed by predicting failure for everything. False Positives (unnecessary inspections) still have a cost, so F1 score — which balances precision and recall — is used to ensure the model remains practical.

Why not accuracy?

The dataset is heavily imbalanced (only ~5.5% failures). A model that predicts "no failure" every time would achieve ~94.5% accuracy while being completely useless. Accuracy is therefore misleading here.

Summary of cost priority from the problem statement:

Prediction Actual Outcome Cost
1 1 TP Repair (medium)
0 1 FN Replacement (highest)
1 0 FP Inspection (lowest)
0 0 TN None

The model should be tuned to prioritize high recall while keeping F1 score acceptable.

Utility Functions¶

In [35]:
def plot(history, name):
    """
    Function to plot loss/accuracy

    history: an object which stores the metrics and losses.
    name: can be one of Loss or Accuracy
    """
    fig, ax = plt.subplots() #Creating a subplot with figure and axes.
    plt.plot(history.history[name]) #Plotting the train accuracy or train loss
    plt.plot(history.history['val_'+name]) #Plotting the validation accuracy or validation loss

    plt.title('Model ' + name.capitalize()) #Defining the title of the plot.
    plt.ylabel(name.capitalize()) #Capitalizing the first letter.
    plt.xlabel('Epoch') #Defining the label for the x-axis.
    fig.legend(['Train', 'Validation'], loc="outside right upper") #Defining the legend, loc controls the position of the legend.
In [36]:
# defining a function to compute different metrics to check performance of a classification model built using statsmodels
def model_performance_classification(
    model, predictors, target, threshold=0.5
):
    """
    Function to compute different metrics to check classification model performance

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    threshold: threshold for classifying the observation as class 1
    """

    # checking which probabilities are greater than threshold
    pred = model.predict(predictors) > threshold
    # pred_temp = model.predict(predictors) > threshold
    # # rounding off the above values to get classes
    # pred = np.round(pred_temp)

    acc = accuracy_score(target, pred)  # to compute Accuracy
    recall = recall_score(target, pred, average='macro')  # to compute Recall
    precision = precision_score(target, pred, average='macro')  # to compute Precision
    f1 = f1_score(target, pred, average='macro')  # to compute F1-score

    # creating a dataframe of metrics
    df_perf = pd.DataFrame(
        {"Accuracy": acc, "Recall": recall, "Precision": precision, "F1 Score": f1,}, index = [0]
    )

    return df_perf

Model 0 — Observations and Insights¶

Architecture

  • Single hidden layer with 64 ReLU units, sigmoid output, SGD optimizer
  • 2,689 trainable parameters — the simplest possible baseline

Loss (Training Curves)

  • Both training and validation loss decrease consistently across all 50 epochs with no divergence
  • Training loss: 0.2425 → 0.0511 (79% reduction)
  • Validation loss: 0.1617 → 0.0611 (62% reduction)
  • Validation loss remains slightly above training loss throughout, which is normal
  • No overfitting observed — the validation loss tracks training loss and never rises

Recall (During Training)

  • Train recall: 0.076 → 0.830
  • Val recall: 0.149 → 0.824
  • Learning is rapid in epochs 1–15 (recall jumps from ~0.08 to ~0.71), then slows after epoch 30
  • Both metrics are still improving at epoch 50 — the model has not fully converged

Final Model Performance

Set Accuracy Recall (macro) Precision (macro) F1 Score (macro)
Train 0.9899 0.9146 0.9884 0.9481
Validation 0.9893 0.9116 0.9842 0.9446

Classification Report — Failure class (Class 1) only:

Set Precision Recall F1 Support
Train 0.99 0.83 0.90 888
Validation 0.98 0.82 0.89 222
  • The model identifies 83% of training failures and 82% of validation failures
  • Non-failure class (Class 0) achieves near-perfect recall (1.00) on both sets — the model almost never falsely flags a healthy generator
  • Train and validation metrics are very close, confirming the model generalizes well with no overfitting

Business Context

  • 82% recall on Class 1 means ~18% of real failures go undetected, resulting in costly generator replacements
  • For this problem, recall on Class 1 should be as close to 1.0 as possible
  • Model 0 establishes a solid baseline; subsequent models should target higher Class 1 recall through deeper architectures, alternative optimizers (e.g. Adam), class weighting, or adjusted classification thresholds

Model 1 — Observations and Insights¶

Architecture

  • Added a second hidden layer: 64 ReLU → 32 ReLU → sigmoid output, SGD optimizer
  • Parameters grew from 2,689 (Model 0) to 4,737 — nearly double
  • Training time increased from ~37s to ~50s

Loss (Training Curves)

  • Training loss: 0.2613 → 0.0388 (85% reduction, vs 79% for Model 0)
  • Validation loss: 0.1729 → 0.0545 (68% reduction)
  • Both curves still declining at epoch 50 — model has not fully converged
  • Validation loss shows slight flattening and minor fluctuation from epoch 40 onwards, suggesting it is approaching a plateau

Recall (During Training)

  • Train recall: 0.014 → 0.875
  • Val recall: 0.050 → 0.851
  • Faster early learning than Model 0 — by epoch 8, val recall had already reached 0.74

Final Model Performance

  • Adding the second hidden layer produced a meaningful improvement — 3% more failures detected on validation
  • No overfitting observed — train and validation metrics remain close throughout training
  • Model is still learning at epoch 50; more epochs or a deeper architecture may improve results further

Model 2¶

To introduce Regularization in our model, let's set the dropout to 50% after adding the first hidden layer. This step will randomly drop 50% of the neurons before proceeding to the next layer, reducing overfitting.

Model 2 — Observations and Insights¶

Architecture

  • Same two hidden layers as Model 1 (64 ReLU → 32 ReLU → sigmoid), but with a Dropout(0.5) layer inserted after the first hidden layer
  • 5,249 total parameters, SGD optimizer
  • Dropout randomly disables 50% of neurons during training to reduce overfitting

Loss (Training Curves)

  • Training loss: 0.2802 → 0.0559
  • Validation loss: 0.1815 → 0.0569
  • The gap between train and val loss is extremely small (~0.001) — much tighter than Model 1 (gap of ~0.016) — dropout is working as a regularizer
  • Training curve is noticeably noisier and more erratic from epoch 15 onwards — normal with dropout, as random neuron dropping adds noise to gradient updates

Recall (During Training)

  • Train recall: 0.028 → 0.798
  • Val recall: 0.000 → 0.824
  • Validation recall is consistently higher than training recall — the opposite of Models 0 and 1
  • This is a dropout signature: neurons are dropped during training making the training metric appear lower, but all neurons activate at validation time

Key Takeaway

  • Adding 50% dropout hurt performance — Model 2 regressed to Model 0 levels
  • Since Model 1 showed very little overfitting, the aggressive regularization was not needed and simply made training harder
  • A dropout rate of 0.5 is likely too high for this dataset; a lower rate or no dropout may be more appropriate

Model 3¶

As we have are dealing with an imbalance in class distribution, we should also be using class weights to allow the model to give proportionally more importance to the minority class.

In [74]:
# Calculate class weights for imbalanced dataset
cw = (y_train.shape[0]) / np.bincount(y_train.astype(int)) # Convert y_train to integers

# Create a dictionary mapping class indices to their respective class weights
cw_dict = {}
for i in range(cw.shape[0]):
    cw_dict[i] = cw[i]

Model 3 — Observations and Insights¶

Architecture

  • Same as Model 2: 64 ReLU → Dropout(0.5) → 32 ReLU → 16 ReLU → sigmoid, SGD, 5,249 parameters
  • Key addition: class weights applied during training
    • Class 0 (no failure): weight = 1.059
    • Class 1 (failure): weight = 18.018 — every missed failure costs the model 18× more

Loss (Training Curves)

  • Training loss: 0.9144 → 0.3424 — values are much higher than all previous models
  • This is expected: class weights inflate the loss for failure samples, so absolute loss values are not comparable across models
  • Validation loss: 0.2802 → 0.1110
  • Both curves are very noisy and erratic throughout — the combination of dropout and large class weights creates unstable gradient updates
  • Validation loss does not decrease monotonically; it fluctuates between ~0.09 and ~0.28 across epochs

Recall (During Training)

  • Train recall starts at 0.821 at epoch 1 (vs 0.014 for Model 2) — class weights immediately force the model to prioritise failures
  • Train recall: 0.821 → 0.914 by epoch 50
  • Val recall: 0.878 → 0.892
  • Training recall plateaus in a noisy band from ~epoch 20 onwards

Final Model Performance

Set Accuracy Recall (macro) Precision (macro) F1 Score (macro)
Train 0.9915 0.9542 0.9640 0.9590
Validation 0.9908 0.9442 0.9660 0.9548

Classification Report — Failure class (Class 1) only:

Set Precision Recall F1 Support
Train 0.93 0.91 0.92 888
Validation 0.94 0.89 0.91 222
  • Class 1 precision dropped to 0.93–0.94 compared to 0.98–0.99 in previous models — class weighting makes the model more aggressive about predicting failures, catching more but also generating more false positives

Comparison Across All Models (Validation)

Metric Model 0 Model 1 Model 2 Model 3
Class 1 Recall 0.82 0.85 0.82 0.89
Class 1 Precision 0.98 0.98 0.98 0.94
Class 1 F1 0.89 0.91 0.89 0.91
Macro Recall 0.9116 0.9251 0.9116 0.9442

Key Takeaway

  • Class weighting is the most impactful change so far — Class 1 recall improved from 0.85 (Model 1 best) to 0.89
  • The model learns to prioritise failures from the very first epoch, unlike previous models which started near zero recall
  • The trade-off: precision on Class 1 dropped (0.94 vs 0.98), meaning more false positives — unnecessary inspections increase, but replacement costs decrease
  • For this business problem, that is an acceptable trade-off since inspection costs are the lowest of the three cost types

Model 4¶

Since we have used only SGD optimizer till now, let's use another kind of optimizer and observe its impact on the model performmance.

Model 5 — Observations and Insights¶

Architecture

  • Larger network: 128 ReLU → Dropout(0.5) → 64 ReLU → 32 ReLU → sigmoid
  • Adam optimizer — first model to use Adam instead of SGD
  • 15,617 parameters — 3× larger than Models 2–3
  • No class weights

Loss (Training Curves)

  • Training loss: 0.1369 → 0.0353
  • Validation loss: 0.0728 → 0.0552
  • Both curves drop steeply in the first ~10 epochs then plateau — Adam converges much faster than SGD
  • Train loss (0.035) is noticeably lower than val loss (0.055) by epoch 50 — a wider gap than previous models, indicating mild overfitting from the larger network

Recall (During Training)

  • Train recall: 0.409 → 0.892
  • Val recall: 0.730 at epoch 1 — Adam reaches in a single epoch what SGD took ~10 epochs to achieve
  • Val recall: 0.730 → 0.874 by epoch 50
  • Both curves plateau from ~epoch 15 onwards, fluctuating in a narrow band with no further improvement

Final Model Performance

Key Takeaway

  • Adam converges dramatically faster than SGD — val recall of 0.73 in the very first epoch
  • Best Class 1 F1 score so far (0.93) with strong precision (0.98) — no precision trade-off unlike Model 3
  • Class 1 recall (0.88) is marginally below Model 3 (0.89) — class weights still give Model 3 the edge on catching failures
  • For the business goal of maximising recall, Model 3 still leads; for balancing precision and recall, Model 5 is the strongest model so far

Observations on Model 6¶

Architecture:

  • 4-layer dense network: 128 → 64 → 32 → 1 (sigmoid output)
  • Dropout (0.5) after the first layer
  • Adam optimizer with binary crossentropy loss; primary metric is Recall
  • Class weights {0: 1, 1: 5} applied to bias the model toward the minority class (class 1 = failure)

Performance Summary:

Metric Train Validation
Accuracy 99.49% 99.25%
Recall 96.07% 94.52%
Precision 98.99% 98.21%
F1 Score 97.48% 96.28%

Classification Report — Failure class (Class 1):

Set Precision Recall F1
Train 0.98 0.92 0.95
Validation 0.97 0.89 0.93

Key Observations:

  1. Fast convergence with Adam — the model achieved recall of ~0.90 on both train and validation from epoch 1, compared to SGD models that required 10–15 epochs to reach similar levels. This is consistent with Adam's adaptive learning rate.
  2. Strong minority class recall — class weights {0:1, 1:5} successfully prioritize class 1, achieving Class 1 recall of 0.92 on training and 0.89 on validation — the highest failure recall across all models.
  3. No significant overfitting — the train/validation gap is small across all metrics (~1.5% on recall, ~0.8% on F1), indicating that dropout is effectively regularizing the model despite its larger size.
  4. High precision maintained — precision of 0.97–0.98 on class 1 means very few false alarms, keeping unnecessary inspection costs low while still catching the majority of failures.
  5. Improvement over Model 5 (Adam, no class weights) — adding class weights improved class 1 recall from 0.88 to 0.89 on validation while maintaining similar precision, confirming that class weighting adds meaningful benefit on top of the Adam optimizer.

Checking the performance of the best model on the test set

Model 5 wins on F1 and accuracy, but since catching real failures (recall) is the priority for ReneWind — missing a turbine failure is more costly than a false alarm — Model 6's recall advantage takes precedence. The F1 tiebreaker doesn't come into play here because Model 6 clearly leads on the primary metric.

Actionable Insights and Recommendations¶

Conclusions and Insights for ReneWind¶

Business Impact¶

The model catches 88% of generator failures before they occur, converting what would be costly unplanned replacements into scheduled repairs. The remaining 12% of failures go undetected — an accepted limitation given the data available. False alarms (flagging a healthy turbine) result only in an inspection, the lowest-cost outcome, and occur at a manageable rate with 94% precision.

What the Modeling Revealed¶

  • No single sensor strongly predicts failure — the highest individual correlation was 0.29. Generator failure is a multivariate problem that requires a model capable of learning complex interactions across all 40 sensors simultaneously.
  • Class imbalance (only 5.5% of observations are failures) is the central modeling challenge. Standard models ignore the minority class; class weighting was the single most impactful technique, improving failure detection by 4 percentage points.
  • The Adam optimizer dramatically outperforms SGD for this problem — achieving near-optimal recall within the first few training epochs.
  • Larger networks with dropout regularization generalize better and avoid overfitting despite the imbalanced data.

Recommendation to ReneWind¶

Model 6 is the recommended model. It best aligns with the business cost structure — prioritizing recall to minimize replacements while keeping false alarm rates acceptable. The combination of a deeper network, Adam optimizer, dropout, and class weighting represents the optimal configuration given this dataset.
